l: The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra / Chapter 1
s: In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, the LORD stirred Cyrus's spirit to fulfill the word spoken by Jeremiah, and Cyrus issued a written proclamation throughout his kingdom. The proclamation said the LORD, the God of heaven, had given him all the kingdoms and commanded him to build a house in Jerusalem, and it invited any of God's people to go up and build it, with neighbors helping with silver, gold, goods, and animals. The heads of fathers' households of Judah and Benjamin, with the priests and Levites, whose spirits God had stirred, rose up to go and build, and those around them strengthened their hands with gifts. Cyrus also brought out the vessels of the LORD's house, which Nebuchadnezzar had carried off to the house of his gods, and counted them out through Mithredath the treasurer to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah. The vessels totaled five thousand four hundred, and Sheshbazzar brought them up to Jerusalem when the captives were brought up from Babylon.

l: Cyrus, The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra / Chapter 1
s: In his first year, Cyrus's spirit was stirred by the LORD, and he issued a written proclamation throughout his kingdom saying the God of heaven had given him all the kingdoms and commanded him to build a house in Jerusalem. He also brought out the vessels of the LORD's house through Mithredath the treasurer and had them counted out to Sheshbazzar.

l: LORD, The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra / Chapter 1
s: The LORD fulfilled his word spoken by Jeremiah by stirring up the spirit of Cyrus, and he also stirred the spirits of the heads of households, priests, and Levites to go up and build. He is identified in Cyrus's proclamation as the God of heaven and the God of Israel, who commanded that a house be built for him in Jerusalem.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra / Chapter 1
s: Jerusalem, in Judah, is named as the place where the LORD's house is to be built, according to Cyrus's proclamation. It is the destination to which the people went up and to which Sheshbazzar brought the vessels.

l: Sheshbazzar, The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra / Chapter 1
s: Sheshbazzar, called the prince of Judah, was given the vessels of the LORD's house, counted out to him by Mithredath the treasurer at Cyrus's order. He brought all of them up to Jerusalem when the captives were brought up from Babylon.

l: house of God at Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra / Chapter 1
s: Cyrus declared that the LORD commanded him to build a house for him in Jerusalem, and invited God's people to go up and build it. The heads of households, priests, and Levites rose up to build it, supported by gifts of silver, gold, goods, animals, and precious things, plus freewill offerings.

l: heads of fathers' households (of Judah and Benjamin), The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra / Chapter 1
s: The heads of fathers' households of Judah and Benjamin, together with the priests and Levites, rose up to go to Jerusalem and build the LORD's house, because God had stirred their spirits. Those around them strengthened their hands with vessels of silver, gold, goods, animals, and precious things.

l: captives (brought up from Babylon), The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra / Chapter 1
s: The captives were brought up from Babylon to Jerusalem. Sheshbazzar brought the vessels of the LORD's house up at that time.

l: gold and silver vessels of God's house, The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra / Chapter 1
s: The vessels had been brought out of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar and put in the house of his gods. Cyrus brought them out and had them counted to Sheshbazzar: thirty gold platters, a thousand silver platters, twenty-nine knives, thirty gold bowls, 410 silver bowls of a second kind, and a thousand other vessels, five thousand four hundred in all of gold and silver, and Sheshbazzar brought them up to Jerusalem.

l: Cyrus's proclamation, The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra / Chapter 1
s: The proclamation was made throughout Cyrus's kingdom and put in writing. It stated that the LORD had given Cyrus all the kingdoms and commanded him to build a house in Jerusalem, invited any of God's people to go up and build, and directed that those remaining in any place help the travelers with silver, gold, goods, and animals, in addition to the freewill offering for God's house.

l: The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 2
s: Chapter 2 lists the children of the province who went up out of captivity in Babylon, where Nebuchadnezzar had carried them, and returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own city. They came with leaders including Zerubbabel and Jeshua. The chapter records the numbers of the men of Israel by family and town, then the priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, and Solomon's servants. Some priestly families who could not prove their genealogy were disqualified, and the governor barred them from the most holy things until a priest could serve with Urim and Thummim. The whole assembly numbered 42,360, besides servants, singers, and animals; some heads of households gave willingly to the work of God's house, and all settled in their cities.

l: Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 2
s: Zerubbabel is named first among the leaders with whom the returning people came up from captivity, along with Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, and others.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 2
s: Jerusalem is the destination to which the exiles returned from Babylon, each to his own city. The LORD's house is located there, and it is where some heads of households gave willingly for the work.

l: returning exiles (children of the province), The Book of Ezra, Chapter 2
s: The children of the province went up out of the captivity to which Nebuchadnezzar had carried them and returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his city. They are listed by family and town, and the whole assembly totaled 42,360, besides 7,337 male and female servants and 200 singing men and women. They also had 736 horses, 245 mules, 435 camels, and 6,720 donkeys. At the end, the priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, and some of the people lived in their cities, and all Israel in theirs.

l: priests (Jeshua's brothers), The Book of Ezra, Chapter 2
s: The priests are listed as the children of Jedaiah (973), Immer (1,052), Pashhur (1,247), and Harim (1,017). The children of Habaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai could not find their registration in the genealogies and were deemed disqualified and removed from the priesthood. The governor told them not to eat the most holy things until a priest stood up with Urim and Thummim. The priests gave 100 priests' garments to the treasury and afterward lived in their cities.

l: house of God at Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 2
s: The LORD's house in Jerusalem is the place to which some heads of fathers' households came and then offered willingly to set it up in its place.

l: freewill offering for the temple, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 2
s: Some heads of fathers' households offered willingly for God's house to set it up in its place. According to their ability they gave into the treasury 61,000 darics of gold, 5,000 minas of silver, and 100 priests' garments.

l: return from Babylonian captivity, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 2
s: Those whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away to Babylon went up out of captivity and returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own city, with Zerubbabel and other leaders. Some who came from Tel Melah, Tel Harsha, Cherub, Addan, and Immer could not show their fathers' houses or prove they were of Israel. The return ends with the people settled in their cities.

l: census of returnees, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 2
s: The chapter gives a detailed count of the men of Israel by family and town, followed by priests (3,289 by the listed families), Levites (74), singers (128), gatekeepers (139), and temple servants with Solomon's servants (392). The whole assembly is totaled at 42,360, with 7,337 servants and 200 singers counted separately, plus livestock totals for horses, mules, camels, and donkeys.

l: The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 3
s: In the seventh month the people of Israel gathered at Jerusalem as one man, and Jeshua the son of Jozadak and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, with the priests and their relatives, built the altar and offered burnt offerings on it despite fear of the surrounding peoples. They kept the feast of booths and the set offerings, though the temple foundation was not yet laid. They paid masons and carpenters and gave food, drink, and oil to the people of Sidon and Tyre to bring cedar from Lebanon to Joppa under Cyrus's grant. In the second month of the second year, Zerubbabel, Jeshua, the priests, the Levites, and the returned captives began the work and appointed Levites aged twenty and up to oversee it. When the foundation was laid, priests with trumpets and Levites with cymbals praised the LORD, and the people shouted, while the old men who had seen the first house wept so loudly that the weeping and joyful shouting could not be told apart.

l: Jeshua the son of Jozadak, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 3
s: Jeshua stood up with his brothers the priests and with Zerubbabel and built the altar to offer burnt offerings as written in the law of Moses. In the second year he helped begin the work on the house and stood with his sons and brothers to oversee the workmen.

s: Zerubbabel, with his relatives and Jeshua, built the altar of the God of Israel and offered burnt offerings on it. In the second month of the second year he joined Jeshua, the priests, and the Levites in beginning the work on the LORD's house.

l: priests (Jeshua's brothers), The Book of Ezra, Chapter 3
s: The priests stood with Jeshua to build the altar and offer burnt offerings. When the foundation was laid they were set in their vestments with trumpets to praise the LORD according to David's directions, and many of them wept aloud.

l: Levites, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 3
s: Levites from twenty years old and upward were appointed to oversee the work of the LORD's house, and Kadmiel, the sons of Judah, and the sons of Henadad with their sons and brothers oversaw the workmen. The Levites, the sons of Asaph, played cymbals to praise the LORD at the foundation laying.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 3
s: Jerusalem is where the people gathered in the seventh month and where the altar was built. It is also where the returned captives began work on God's house in the second year of their coming.

l: altar of the God of Israel, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 3
s: The altar was built by Jeshua, Zerubbabel, and their companions as written in the law of Moses. They set it on its base despite fear of the surrounding peoples and offered burnt offerings on it morning and evening.

l: burnt offerings, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 3
s: Burnt offerings were offered on the altar morning and evening, starting from the first day of the seventh month, along with the daily offerings by number, the continual offering, the new moon offerings, the set feasts, and free will offerings. They began before the temple foundation was laid.

l: LORD, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 3
s: The LORD received the burnt offerings and the free will offerings of the people and was praised at the foundation laying as good, with loving kindness enduring forever toward Israel. The returned people acted according to what is written in the law of Moses and the directions of David.

l: house of God at Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 3
s: The foundation was not yet laid when the offerings began in the seventh month. Materials were arranged, with cedar from Lebanon brought by Sidon and Tyre, and the work began in the second month of the second year. The builders then laid the foundation, which was celebrated with praise.

l: old men who had seen the first house, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 3
s: Many of the priests, Levites, and heads of fathers' households who were old men and had seen the first house wept with a loud voice when they saw the new foundation laid. Their weeping mingled with the joyful shouting of others.

l: foundation laying celebration, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 3
s: When the foundation was laid, priests with trumpets and Levites with cymbals praised the LORD, and the people sang antiphonally, saying he is good and his loving kindness endures forever. The great shout of joy mingled with weeping so that the two could not be told apart, and the noise was heard far away.

l: The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 4
s: The adversaries of Judah and Benjamin offer to help build the temple, but Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the heads of fathers' households refuse, citing King Cyrus's command. The people of the land then weaken and trouble the builders and hire counselors against them through the reigns of Cyrus and Darius. In the days of Artaxerxes, Rehum the chancellor, Shimshai the scribe, and their companions write a letter accusing Jerusalem of being a rebellious city that will stop paying tribute if rebuilt. Artaxerxes searches the records, confirms Jerusalem's history of revolt, and orders the building stopped. Rehum, Shimshai, and their companions enforce this by force of arms, and the work on God's house halts until the second year of Darius.

l: Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 4
s: Zerubbabel, together with Jeshua and the other heads of fathers' households, refuses the adversaries' offer to help build the temple. He says they alone will build to the LORD, the God of Israel, as King Cyrus commanded.

l: adversaries of Judah and Benjamin, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 4
s: They hear that the captives are building a temple and ask to join, claiming they seek the same God and have sacrificed to him since the days of Esar Haddon king of Assyria. After being refused, they are identified as the people of the land, who weaken the hands of Judah, trouble the builders, and hire counselors against them to frustrate the work.

l: Jews, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 4
s: The children of the captivity are building a temple to the LORD, the God of Israel. They reject outside help, are then troubled and weakened by the people of the land, and are finally made to stop by force of arms.

l: house of God at Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 4
s: The temple is being built when the adversaries offer help and are refused, and it is then opposed for years. Its construction stops after Artaxerxes' order and remains stopped until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.

l: Artaxerxes, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 4
s: Artaxerxes king of Persia receives the letter from Rehum, Shimshai, and their companions. He has the records searched, finds that Jerusalem rebelled in the past and was ruled by mighty kings who received tribute, and decrees that the men cease and the city not be built until he makes a decree.

l: Rehum, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 4
s: Rehum the chancellor, with Shimshai the scribe, writes a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes. He receives the king's answer ordering the building stopped, and then goes in haste to Jerusalem with his companions to make the Jews cease by force of arms.

l: Shimshai, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 4
s: Shimshai the scribe joins Rehum in writing the letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes. He is addressed in the king's reply and helps enforce the stop order at Jerusalem.

l: companions of Rehum and Shimshai, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 4
s: Named as the Dinaites, Apharsathchites, Tarpelites, Apharsites, Archevites, Babylonians, Shushanchites, Dehaites, Elamites, and the rest of the nations Osnappar settled in Samaria and beyond the River, they join in writing the letter. They go in haste to Jerusalem after the king's reply and stop the Jews by force of arms.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 4
s: Jerusalem is accused in the letter of being a rebellious and bad city that has started rebellions before and would withhold tribute if rebuilt. Artaxerxes' search of the records confirms its past insurrections and its former mighty kings, and he orders that it not be built until he decrees otherwise.

l: letter of accusation to Artaxerxes, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 4
s: Written in Syrian by Rehum, Shimshai, and their companions, the letter says the Jews are rebuilding walls and foundations and warns the king he will lose his possession beyond the River. It urges a search of the records of the king's fathers. It succeeds in prompting Artaxerxes' order to halt the building.

l: stopping of the temple work, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 4
s: After Artaxerxes' letter is read before Rehum, Shimshai, and their companions, they go to Jerusalem and make the Jews cease by force of arms. Work on God's house stops and does not resume until the second year of Darius king of Persia.

l: The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 5
s: Haggai and Zechariah prophesy to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem, and Zerubbabel and Jeshua begin building God's house with the prophets' help. Tattenai, the governor beyond the River, and Shetharbozenai question the builders about who authorized the work and ask for their names, but they are not able to stop it because God's eye is on the elders. Tattenai and his companions write to King Darius, reporting that the work is prospering and relaying the elders' account. The elders say they serve the God of heaven and earth, that the house was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar after the people provoked God, and that Cyrus decreed its rebuilding and sent the vessels with Sheshbazzar, who laid the foundations. The letter asks Darius to search the treasure house at Babylon for Cyrus's decree and to send his decision.

l: Jews, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 5
s: The Jews in Judah and Jerusalem are prophesied to by Haggai and Zechariah in the name of the God of Israel. They are questioned by Tattenai about who authorized their building, and the work continues while the matter is referred to Darius.

l: LORD, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 5
s: Haggai and Zechariah prophesy in his name to the Jews. His eye is on the elders of the Jews, so the governor's officials do not make them stop building. The elders describe him as the God of heaven and earth, who in wrath gave their fathers into Nebuchadnezzar's hand.

l: house of God at Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 5
s: Zerubbabel and Jeshua begin to build it, and it is reported to be going up with great stones and timber in the walls, prospering in the builders' hands. The elders explain it was built long ago by a great king of Israel, destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, and its foundations were later laid by Sheshbazzar. It is still not completed.

l: Tattenai, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 5
s: Tattenai, the governor beyond the River, comes with Shetharbozenai and their companions to ask the Jews who authorized the building and for the names of the builders. He sends a letter to Darius reporting what he saw and heard, and asks that a search be made for Cyrus's decree.

l: elders of the Jews, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 5
s: The elders are watched over by God's eye, so they are not made to stop building. They answer Tattenai that they are servants of the God of heaven and earth, recount the temple's destruction and Cyrus's decree, and give their names as requested.

l: Darius, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 5
s: Darius is the king to whom Tattenai and his companions send their letter. He is asked to search the king's treasure house at Babylon for Cyrus's decree and to send his pleasure concerning the matter.

l: letter to Darius, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 5
s: Tattenai, Shetharbozenai, and their companions the Apharsachites send it to Darius with greetings of peace. It reports that the house is being built diligently with great stones and timber, relays the elders' account including the claim of Cyrus's decree, and requests a search of the Babylon treasure house.

l: decree to build the house, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 5
s: The Jewish elders claim that Cyrus made a decree in his first year to build God's house. Tattenai asks who gave the decree, and his letter requests that Babylon's treasure house be searched to verify whether Cyrus made it. Its existence is not yet confirmed in this unit.

l: Cyrus, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 5
s: According to the elders, Cyrus, called king of Babylon, made a decree in his first year to build God's house. He took the gold and silver vessels Nebuchadnezzar had carried off from the Babylon temple and delivered them to Sheshbazzar, whom he had made governor, with instructions to put them in the Jerusalem temple.

l: Sheshbazzar, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 5
s: The elders say Cyrus made Sheshbazzar governor and delivered to him the temple vessels, telling him to place them in the temple in Jerusalem and have God's house built in its place. He came and laid the foundations of God's house.

l: The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 6
s: King Darius orders a search of the archives in Babylon, and a scroll is found at Achmetha in Media recording Cyrus's decree in his first year that God's house at Jerusalem be rebuilt at royal expense, with its vessels restored. Darius reaffirms the decree, orders Tattenai, Shetharbozenai and their companions to stay away and to supply the Jews' needs, and pronounces penalties on anyone who alters it. Tattenai and his companions comply diligently, and the elders of the Jews build and finish the house through the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah the son of Iddo, on the third day of Adar in Darius's sixth year. The children of Israel, priests and Levites dedicate the house with joy and many offerings, and set the priests and Levites in their divisions. They then keep the Passover and the feast of unleavened bread for seven days, rejoicing because the LORD had strengthened their hands.

l: Darius the king, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 6
s: Darius orders the archives searched and, after the scroll of Cyrus's decree is found, issues his own decree confirming it. He commands the governors beyond the River to leave the work alone and fund it, and threatens those who alter the decree. His sixth year is when the house is finished.

l: Cyrus, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 6
s: A scroll found at Achmetha records that in his first year Cyrus decreed the rebuilding of God's house at Jerusalem. He ordered the expenses paid from the king's house and the vessels taken by Nebuchadnezzar restored. His decree is cited as one of the authorities behind the completed building.

l: decree to build the house, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 6
s: The decree is found in a scroll at Achmetha in the province of Media. It specifies a house sixty cubits high and wide, with three courses of great stones and a course of new timber, paid for by the king's house, and the return of the gold and silver vessels. Darius confirms it and the building is completed according to it.

l: house of God at Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 6
s: The house is rebuilt under the decrees of Cyrus and Darius, with royal funding and the return of its vessels. The elders finish it on the third day of Adar in the sixth year of Darius. It is then dedicated with joy and sacrifices, and the priests and Levites are set in their divisions for service there.

l: Tattenai, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 6
s: Tattenai, governor beyond the River, is told in the decree to stay far away and leave the work alone, and to give expenses to the Jewish elders. He and Shetharbozenai and their companions comply with all diligence because Darius had sent the decree.

l: elders of the Jews, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 6
s: The elders are authorized to build the house in its place and are to receive expenses from the king's goods. They build and prosper through the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah the son of Iddo, and finish the house.

l: LORD, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 6
s: The decree provides bulls, rams, lambs, wheat, salt, wine and oil so sacrifices of pleasant aroma may be offered to the God of heaven, with prayer for the king and his sons. Darius calls on the God who caused his name to dwell at Jerusalem to overthrow any who alter the decree or destroy the house.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 6
s: The children of Israel, with the priests, Levites and the rest of the captivity, dedicate the house with joy and offer one hundred bulls, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs and twelve male goats as a sin offering. Those who had returned, together with others who separated from the nations' filthiness to seek the LORD, keep the Passover and the feast of unleavened bread.

l: dedication of the temple, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 6
s: The house is dedicated with joy by the children of Israel, priests, Levites and the rest of the captivity. They offer one hundred bulls, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs and twelve male goats according to the number of the tribes. They set the priests and Levites in their divisions as written in the book of Moses.

l: Passover, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 6
s: The children of the captivity keep the Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month. The priests and Levites had purified themselves and killed the Passover for all the returned exiles, their brothers the priests, and themselves. It is followed by seven days of the feast of unleavened bread with joy.

l: The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 7
s: Chapter 7 introduces Ezra, a priest descended from Aaron through a listed genealogy and a skilled scribe in the law of Moses, who went up from Babylon to Jerusalem in the seventh year of King Artaxerxes of Persia. He left on the first day of the first month and arrived on the first day of the fifth month, because the good hand of his God was on him and he had set his heart to seek, do, and teach the LORD's law. The chapter reproduces Artaxerxes' letter, which permits willing Israelites, priests, and Levites to go with Ezra, sends silver and gold for offerings at the house of God in Jerusalem, and orders the treasurers beyond the River to supply Ezra's needs. The letter also exempts temple personnel from tribute, tells Ezra to appoint magistrates and judges, and prescribes penalties for those who do not keep the law of God and the law of the king. Ezra closes by blessing the LORD for putting this in the king's heart and describes gathering chief men of Israel to go up with him.

l: Ezra, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 7
s: Ezra, son of Seraiah and a descendant of Aaron the chief priest, is introduced as a priest and a skilled scribe in the law of Moses. He had set his heart to seek the LORD's law, to do it, and to teach statutes and ordinances in Israel, and the king granted all his requests. He led the journey from Babylon to Jerusalem, was commissioned by the king's letter to appoint judges and carry offerings, and blessed the LORD for the king's favor before gathering chief men of Israel to go with him.

l: Artaxerxes, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 7
s: Artaxerxes, king of Persia, in his seventh year granted Ezra all his request and wrote a letter calling himself king of kings. He decreed that willing Israelites could go to Jerusalem, supplied silver, gold, and further resources from the royal treasury, exempted temple personnel from taxes, and ordered judgment on any who disobey the law of God or the king. He explained his generosity by asking why wrath should fall on his realm and his sons.

l: LORD, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 7
s: The LORD, the God of Israel, is said to have given the law of Moses, and his good hand was on Ezra throughout the journey and the king's favor. Artaxerxes' letter calls him the God of heaven and the God of Jerusalem and speaks of wrath against the realm if his commands are not done. Ezra blesses him as the God of our fathers who put it in the king's heart to beautify his house in Jerusalem.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 7
s: Jerusalem is the destination of Ezra and the Israelites, priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants who went up from Babylon in the seventh year of Artaxerxes. Ezra arrived there on the first day of the fifth month. The king sent him to inquire concerning Judah and Jerusalem according to the law of his God, and it is described as the habitation of the God of Israel.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 7
s: Some of the children of Israel, including priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants, went up to Jerusalem with Ezra. Artaxerxes' decree allowed any of the people of Israel in his realm to go willingly. Ezra had set his heart to teach statutes and ordinances in Israel, and he gathered chief men out of Israel to go up with him.

l: law of Moses, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 7
s: The law of Moses is described as given by the LORD, the God of Israel, and Ezra is a skilled scribe in it. The letter refers to it as the law of Ezra's God, which is in his hand, and Ezra is to use it to inquire about Judah and Jerusalem and to appoint judges who know it. Ezra is also to teach those who do not know it, and those who will not do it face judgment.

l: house of God at Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 7
s: The house of God in Jerusalem is the purpose of the silver, gold, vessels, and free will offerings that Ezra is to carry. The king commands that bulls, rams, and lambs with their meal and drink offerings be bought and offered on its altar, and that further needs be met from the king's treasury. Its personnel are exempt from tribute, custom, and toll, and Ezra blesses the LORD for putting it in the king's heart to beautify it.

l: silver, gold, and vessels offering, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 7
s: The king and his counselors freely offered silver and gold to the God of Israel, and Ezra was to carry it along with whatever he found in the province of Babylon and the free will offerings of the people and priests. It was to buy offerings for the altar, and what remained could be used as Ezra and his brothers saw fit according to God's will. The treasurers beyond the River were also to supply up to one hundred talents of silver on Ezra's request.

l: Ezra's journey to Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 7
s: Ezra began going up from Babylon on the first day of the first month and reached Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month in the seventh year of Artaxerxes. The text attributes the success of the journey to the good hand of his God on him. He was accompanied by some Israelites, priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants, along with chief men he gathered out of Israel.

l: Artaxerxes' letter, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 7
s: The letter, given to Ezra the priest and scribe, decrees that willing Israelites, priests, and Levites may go with him and that he is sent by the king and his seven counselors to inquire about Judah and Jerusalem. It directs the carrying and use of silver and gold, orders the treasurers beyond the River to supply Ezra up to set amounts of silver, wheat, wine, oil, and unlimited salt, and exempts temple workers from taxes. It also instructs Ezra to appoint magistrates and judges and prescribes death, banishment, confiscation, or imprisonment for those who disobey the law of God and the king.

l: The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 8
s: Chapter 8 lists the heads of fathers' households and the males with them who went up from Babylon with the narrator in the reign of Artaxerxes. At the river Ahava the narrator found no sons of Levi among the people, so he sent chief men and teachers to Iddo at Casiphia, and they brought back Sherebiah, Hashabiah, their kin, and 220 temple servants. The narrator proclaimed a fast at Ahava to seek a straight way, since he was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers, and God granted their request. He set apart twelve chiefs of the priests, including Sherebiah and Hashabiah, and weighed to them the silver, gold, and vessels offered for God's house. After leaving Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month, the group was delivered from enemies and bandits, reached Jerusalem, and on the fourth day weighed the treasure into the hand of Meremoth, offered sacrifices, and delivered the king's commissions to the governors.

l: Ezra, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 8
s: The text's first-person narrator, who is not named in this unit, lists the households that went up with him from Babylon and gathers them at the river Ahava. He finds no Levites there, sends for ministers, proclaims a fast, entrusts the offering to twelve priestly chiefs, and leads the group to Jerusalem, where he delivers the king's commissions.

l: Ahava river, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 8
s: The river that runs to Ahava is where the narrator gathered the returning company and they encamped three days. There he found no Levites, proclaimed the fast, and weighed out the offering, and the company departed from it on the twelfth day of the first month.

l: LORD, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 8
s: God's good hand is credited with bringing Sherebiah and the Levites, and he granted the request of those who fasted and begged him. His hand was on the company so that he delivered them from the enemy and the bandits on the way. The narrator recalls telling the king that God's hand is for good on all who seek him, while his power and wrath are against all who forsake him.

l: Sherebiah, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 8
s: Sherebiah, a man of discretion of the sons of Mahli, son of Levi, was brought from Casiphia with his sons and brothers, eighteen in all. He was then set apart as one of twelve chiefs of the priests to receive the weighed silver, gold, and vessels.

l: Hashabiah, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 8
s: Hashabiah came with Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari, along with his brothers and their sons, twenty in all. He was set apart with Sherebiah and ten of their brothers as one of the twelve chiefs entrusted with the offering.

l: Levites, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 8
s: The narrator found no sons of Levi in the company at Ahava, so he sent to Iddo at Casiphia for ministers for God's house. Sherebiah, Hashabiah, their kin, and 220 temple servants given by David and the princes for the Levites' service came. In Jerusalem, the Levites Jozabad son of Jeshua and Noadiah son of Binnui were present when the treasure was weighed.

l: priests, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 8
s: Twelve of the chiefs of the priests, including Sherebiah and Hashabiah, were set apart to receive the silver, gold, and vessels, and were told they and the vessels were holy to the LORD. In Jerusalem the treasure was weighed into the hand of Meremoth the son of Uriah the priest, with Eleazar son of Phinehas.

l: fast at Ahava, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 8
s: The narrator proclaimed this fast at the river Ahava so the people could humble themselves and seek from God a straight way for themselves, their little ones, and their possessions. It followed his shame at asking the king for soldiers and horsemen. The people fasted and begged God, and he granted their request.

l: silver, gold, and vessels offering, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 8
s: The offering from the king, his counselors, his princes, and all Israel present was weighed out at Ahava: 650 talents of silver, 100 talents of silver vessels, 100 talents of gold, twenty gold bowls weighing 1,000 darics, and two vessels of fine bright bronze. The priests and Levites guarded it as a holy free will offering until it was weighed in Jerusalem on the fourth day into Meremoth's hand, with everything counted and the weight written down.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 8
s: The company arrived in Jerusalem and stayed three days. On the fourth day the offering was weighed in the house of God, burnt offerings were made, and the king's commissions were delivered to the governors, who supported the people and God's house.

l: returning exiles, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 8
s: The heads of households and their males who went up from Babylon in Artaxerxes' reign are listed, with counts ranging from fifty to two hundred eighteen. The children of the captivity offered twelve bulls for all Israel, ninety-six rams, seventy-seven lambs, and twelve male goats as a sin offering, all as a burnt offering to the LORD.

l: journey from Ahava to Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 8
s: The company left the river Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month to go to Jerusalem. God's hand was on them and delivered them from the enemy and bandits along the way. They reached Jerusalem and stayed three days before weighing the treasure.

l: The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 9
s: The princes report to the narrator that the people of Israel, the priests, and the Levites have not separated from the peoples of the lands and have taken their daughters as wives for themselves and their sons, with the princes and rulers leading in this trespass. The narrator tears his garment and robe, pulls hair from his head and beard, and sits confounded until the evening offering while those who tremble at God's words gather to him. At the evening offering he falls on his knees, spreads his hands to the LORD, and prays a confession of shame over Israel's long guilt. He recalls the LORD's grace in leaving a remnant and giving favor before the kings of Persia, and cites the prophetic commandment against giving or taking daughters in marriage with the peoples of the land. He asks whether they should break the commandments again, and concludes that the LORD is righteous and that no one can stand before him in their guiltiness.

l: Ezra, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 9
s: Ezra, speaking in the first person, hears the princes' report, tears his garment and robe, pulls out hair from his head and beard, and sits confounded until the evening offering. He then kneels, spreads his hands to the LORD, and offers a prayer confessing the people's guilt and acknowledging the LORD's righteousness.

l: LORD, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 9
s: The LORD is addressed as the righteous God of Israel who has shown a little grace by leaving a remnant, giving a stake in his holy place, and extending loving kindness before the kings of Persia. He commanded through the prophets that the people not intermarry with the peoples of the land, and has punished Israel less than its iniquities deserve.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 9
s: The people of Israel, along with the priests and Levites, are reported to have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands and to have taken their daughters as wives. Ezra's prayer describes them as a guilty remnant who were earlier delivered to kings, sword, captivity, and plunder, yet have been revived and allowed to rebuild the house of God.

l: princes and rulers, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 9
s: The princes bring the report of the intermarriage to Ezra. They also admit that the hand of the princes and rulers has been chief in this trespass.

l: peoples of the lands, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 9
s: The peoples of the lands are listed as Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians, and Amorites, and are described as following abominations. The prophetic command describes their land as unclean and filled with their filthiness, and forbids seeking their peace or prosperity.

l: intermarriage, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 9
s: Israelites, including priests, Levites, princes, and rulers, have taken daughters of the peoples of the lands for themselves and their sons, so that the holy offspring have mixed with those peoples. Ezra and his prayer treat this as a trespass against the prophets' commandment and warn that repeating it would provoke the LORD's anger to the point of consuming the remnant.

l: The Book of Ezra, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 10
s: Ezra prays and weeps before God's house, and a great assembly of Israelites joins in weeping. Shecaniah the son of Jehiel confesses that the people have married foreign women and proposes a covenant to put away these wives and their children according to the law. Ezra makes the chiefs of the priests, the Levites, and all Israel swear to do this, then mourns in the room of Jehohanan. A proclamation summons all the exiles to Jerusalem within three days on penalty of forfeiture, and on the twentieth day of the ninth month they gather in the rain, agree to Ezra's call to separate, and arrange for appointed times and local elders and judges to examine each case, despite opposition from Jonathan, Jahzeiah, Meshullam, and Shabbethai. The examination runs from the first day of the tenth month to the first day of the first month, and the chapter lists the priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and other Israelites found to have taken foreign wives, some of whom had children by them.

l: Ezra, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 10
s: Ezra prays, confesses, and weeps before God's house, then makes the chiefs of the priests, the Levites, and all Israel swear to carry out Shecaniah's proposal. He fasts and mourns in Jehohanan's room, tells the assembled people to confess to the LORD and separate from the peoples of the land and the foreign women, and is set apart with heads of fathers' households to examine the matter.

l: Shecaniah the son of Jehiel, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 10
s: Shecaniah, one of the sons of Elam, answers Ezra by admitting that the people have trespassed by marrying foreign women, yet says there is hope for Israel. He proposes a covenant to put away all the wives and their children according to the law, and urges Ezra to arise and act, promising the people's support.

l: LORD, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 10
s: God is the one against whom Israel has trespassed, and the people wish to turn aside his fierce wrath. He is called the LORD, the God of their fathers, whose pleasure the people are told to do, and the covenant is made with him.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 10
s: Israel is described as burdened with increased guilt through marriages to foreign women. All Israel, with its priests and Levites, swears to Ezra to follow the plan, and a very great assembly of men, women, and children weeps bitterly. The chapter lists many families of Israel, including the sons of Parosh, Elam, Zattu, Bebai, Bani, Pahathmoab, Harim, Hashum, and Nebo, as having taken foreign wives.

l: Jews, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 10
s: The children of the captivity are summoned by proclamation to Jerusalem, with forfeiture of possessions and separation from the assembly for anyone who fails to come in three days. They carry out the plan for examining each case, and Ezra mourns over their trespass.

l: foreign women, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 10
s: The foreign women, taken as wives by many men of Israel, are the cause of the trespass and guilt confessed in the chapter. The covenant calls for them to be put away along with their children, and the text notes that some of the men had children by them.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 10
s: Jerusalem is where all the men of Judah and Benjamin gather within three days in response to the proclamation. They sit in the wide place in front of God's house, trembling because of the matter and the great rain.

l: covenant to put away foreign wives, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 10
s: Shecaniah proposes the covenant to put away all foreign wives and the children born of them according to the law and the counsel of those who tremble at God's commandment. Ezra has the chiefs of the priests, the Levites, and all Israel swear to it, and the guilty priests give their hand to put away their wives and offer a ram for their guilt.

l: assembly at Jerusalem, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 10
s: The men of Judah and Benjamin gather on the twentieth day of the ninth month in front of God's house, trembling and soaked by heavy rain. After Ezra's exhortation they answer with a loud voice that they must do as he said, but ask for appointed times and princes, elders, and judges to handle the matter because the people are many and the weather is wet. Jonathan, Jahzeiah, Meshullam, and Shabbethai are the only ones named as opposing or helping the opposition.

l: examination of mixed marriages, The Book of Ezra, Chapter 10
s: Ezra and certain heads of fathers' households sit down on the first day of the tenth month to examine the matter, and finish with all the men who had married foreign women by the first day of the first month. The results name offenders among the priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and many families of Israel, ending with the note that all these had taken foreign wives and some had children by them.

l: The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah / Chapter 1
s: Nehemiah, son of Hacaliah, is in Susa the palace in the twentieth year, in the month Chislev, when his brother Hanani and some men from Judah come to him. They report that the Jewish remnant in the province is in great affliction and reproach, and that Jerusalem's wall is broken down and its gates burned. Nehemiah sits down, weeps, mourns for several days, and fasts and prays before the God of heaven. In his prayer he confesses the sins of Israel, including his own and his father's house, recalls God's word to Moses about scattering and regathering, and asks for mercy before 'this man'. The chapter ends by noting that Nehemiah was cupbearer to the king.

l: Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah / Chapter 1
s: Nehemiah, son of Hacaliah, is in Susa the palace when he asks Hanani and the men from Judah about the Jews and Jerusalem. On hearing of their affliction and the broken wall, he weeps, mourns, fasts, and prays. He confesses sin on behalf of Israel and his own father's house, asks to be granted mercy in the sight of 'this man', and is identified as cupbearer to the king.

l: Hanani, The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah / Chapter 1
s: Hanani, one of Nehemiah's brothers, comes to Nehemiah with certain men out of Judah. In answer to Nehemiah's questions, they report the afflicted state of the remnant and the ruined condition of Jerusalem's wall and gates.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah / Chapter 1
s: Nehemiah asks the visitors about Jerusalem, and is told that its wall is broken down and its gates are burned with fire. This report moves Nehemiah to weeping, mourning, fasting, and prayer.

l: wall of Jerusalem, The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah / Chapter 1
s: The wall of Jerusalem is reported to be broken down, and its gates are burned with fire. This news from Hanani and the men of Judah prompts Nehemiah's grief and prayer.

l: Jews, The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah / Chapter 1
s: Nehemiah asks about the Jews who escaped and were left of the captivity. The visitors report that the remnant there in the province is in great affliction and reproach.

l: God, The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah / Chapter 1
s: God is addressed as the LORD, the God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and loving kindness with those who love him and keep his commandments. Nehemiah recalls his word to Moses that he would scatter those who trespass but gather those who return, and says he redeemed his servants and people by his great power and strong hand.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah / Chapter 1
s: Nehemiah prays day and night for the children of Israel, God's servants, and confesses that they have sinned against God. He says they dealt very corruptly and did not keep the commandments, statutes, or ordinances given to Moses.

l: Nehemiah's prayer, The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah / Chapter 1
s: Nehemiah prays after fasting, appealing to God to listen, confessing the sins of Israel and his own father's house, and recalling the word given to Moses about scattering and gathering. He closes by asking God to prosper him that day and grant him mercy in the sight of this man.

l: The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 2
s: In the twentieth year of Artaxerxes the king, the cupbearer narrator, visibly sad before the king, explains that his ancestral city lies waste with its gates burned. The king asks his request, the narrator prays to the God of heaven, and he asks to be sent to Judah to build the city. The king grants him letters to the governors beyond the River and to Asaph, keeper of the king's forest, for timber, and sends army captains and horsemen with him. After arriving in Jerusalem, the narrator secretly inspects the broken walls by night, then urges the Jews, priests, nobles and rulers to rebuild, and they agree. Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite servant, and Geshem the Arabian ridicule the effort and accuse them of rebelling, but the narrator answers that the God of heaven will prosper the builders and that the opponents have no portion in Jerusalem.

l: Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 2
s: As the king's wine-bearer, the narrator (the text gives no name in this chapter) is asked about his sad face, tells of Jerusalem's ruin, prays, and obtains permission, letters and timber to go to Judah and build. In Jerusalem he secretly inspects the walls by night, then rallies the people to rebuild and answers the mockers by trusting the God of heaven.

l: Artaxerxes, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 2
s: In his twentieth year, Artaxerxes notices the narrator's sadness and asks his request. He grants the request to send him to Judah, asks how long the journey will be, gives letters to the governors beyond the River and to Asaph for timber, and sends army captains and horsemen with him.

l: God, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 2
s: The narrator prays to the God of heaven before answering the king, and credits the king's granting of his requests to the good hand of his God on him. He tells the people of that good hand and declares that the God of heaven will prosper them in building.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 2
s: The city is described as lying waste, the place of the narrator's fathers' tombs, with its gates consumed by fire. The narrator arrives, stays three days, and inspects its broken walls by night before calling the people to rebuild it.

l: wall of Jerusalem, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 2
s: The narrator inspects the broken-down wall at night, going by the valley gate, the jackal's well, the dung gate, the spring gate and the king's pool, where there was no room for his animal to pass. He then urges the people to build it up so they will not be disgraced.

l: Sanballat the Horonite, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 2
s: Sanballat is greatly grieved when he hears that a man has come to seek the welfare of the children of Israel. With Tobiah and Geshem the Arabian he ridicules and despises the builders and asks whether they will rebel against the king, and the narrator tells him he has no portion, right or memorial in Jerusalem.

l: Tobiah the Ammonite, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 2
s: Tobiah, called the Ammonite servant, is grieved exceedingly at the news that someone has come to seek Israel's welfare. He joins Sanballat and Geshem in ridiculing the builders and accusing them of rebelling, and is told he has no portion, right or memorial in Jerusalem.

l: rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 2
s: The narrator proposes the project after secretly inspecting the wall, and the people respond, "Let's rise up and build," strengthening their hands for the good work. It is supported by the king's letters and timber but immediately opposed by Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem, who mock it.

l: The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 3
s: Chapter 3 lists the many people and groups who rebuilt and repaired the wall and gates of Jerusalem, section by section. Eliashib the high priest and his fellow priests started the work at the sheep gate, and the sons of Hassenaah, Hanun with the people of Zanoah, Malchijah son of Rechab, and Shallun built the fish, valley, dung, and spring gates, along with the old gate. Rulers of districts, goldsmiths, perfumers, merchants, Levites, temple servants' neighbors, and families working across from their own houses each repaired assigned portions. The Tekoites repaired two sections, though their nobles would not put their necks to the Lord's work. The listing ends where it began, with the goldsmiths and merchants repairing between the ascent of the corner and the sheep gate.

l: Eliashib the high priest, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 3
s: Eliashib the high priest rose up with his brothers the priests and built the sheep gate, sanctifying it and setting up its doors. His house is also named as a landmark, with Baruch repairing from the turning of the wall to its door and Meremoth repairing along the house from its door to its end.

l: priests, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 3
s: The priests, led by Eliashib, built and sanctified the sheep gate and the wall to the towers of Hammeah and Hananel. Later, the priests from the surrounding area made repairs, and the priests repaired above the horse gate, each across from his own house.

l: sheep gate, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 3
s: The sheep gate was built by Eliashib and the priests, who sanctified it and set up its doors. It is also where the chapter's account of repairs closes, with the goldsmiths and merchants working between the ascent of the corner and the sheep gate.

l: Tekoites, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 3
s: The Tekoites made repairs on one section of the wall, but their nobles did not put their necks to the Lord's work. They later repaired another portion opposite the great tower that stands out, as far as the wall of Ophel.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 3
s: Jerusalem is the city whose wall and gates are repaired in this chapter, and it is divided into districts. Rephaiah son of Hur and Shallum son of Hallohesh each ruled half of the district of Jerusalem, and Shallum made repairs with his daughters.

l: rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 3
s: The wall rebuilding is carried out in assigned sections by priests, rulers, Levites, craftsmen, merchants, families, and townspeople from places such as Jericho, Tekoa, Gibeon, Mizpah, Zanoah, Beth Zur, and Keilah. Many worked across from their own houses, and the gates were built with beams, doors, bolts, and bars. The work went all the way around from the sheep gate and back to it.

l: The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 4
s: Sanballat and Tobiah the Ammonite mock the Jews who are rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem, and the narrator prays that God will turn their reproach back on them. The people keep building until the wall reaches half its height, which angers Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabians, the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites, who conspire to attack Jerusalem. The narrator responds with prayer and a watch, then posts armed guards by family groups and urges the nobles, rulers, and people not to fear but to remember the Lord. After the enemies learn their plan is known and God has frustrated it, the work resumes with half the servants building and half holding weapons, builders working with one hand and holding a weapon with the other, and a trumpeter stationed by the narrator to rally the people. The narrator also has everyone lodge inside Jerusalem to guard at night and work by day, and he and his men do not take off their clothes.

l: Sanballat the Horonite, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 4
s: Sanballat hears of the wall-building, becomes angry and indignant, and mocks the Jews before his brothers and the army of Samaria. Later he joins Tobiah, the Arabians, the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites in becoming very angry and conspiring to fight against Jerusalem.

l: Tobiah the Ammonite, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 4
s: Tobiah the Ammonite stands beside Sanballat and scoffs that if a fox climbed the Jews' stone wall, it would break it down. He later joins the others in anger and in the conspiracy against Jerusalem.

l: Jews, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 4
s: The Jews are mocked as feeble, yet they keep building because they have a mind to work. Judah complains that the burden bearers are fading and the rubble is great, and Jews living near the enemy warn ten times that attacks will come from every direction. They then work armed, half holding weapons while half build.

l: wall of Jerusalem, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 4
s: The wall is mocked as flimsy but is built up until it is joined together to half its height. The breaches begin to be filled, which provokes the enemies to plot against the city.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 4
s: Jerusalem is the target of the enemy conspiracy to fight against it and cause confusion. The narrator orders that everyone with his servant lodge within the city so they can guard it at night and labor by day.

l: God, The Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 4
s: God is asked by the narrator to hear the prayer, to turn the enemies' reproach on their own heads, and not to blot out their sin. He is described as great and awesome, is said to have brought the enemy counsel to nothing, and is promised to fight for the people.
